sentences.text: Rajasaurus was a robust carnivorous abelisaurid theropod dinosaur from India, estimated to measure approximately 6.6 meters in length.
This predator stood about 2.4 meters tall and weighed between 400 and 700 kilograms.
It is distinguished by a single horn on its forehead, elongated supratemporal fenestrae, and iliac crests that separate the brevis platform from the hip joint.
The frontal bones of its braincase reached a maximum thickness of 4 centimeters above the eye socket.
The fossil site in Balasinor is known as the "Jurassic Park of India" due to its popularity with tourists.
Rajasaurus appears in the Prehistoric Planet episode "Badlands," hunting Isisaurus hatchlings in the Deccan Traps.
The genus Rajasaurus was named by Wilson and colleagues in 2003 based on bones discovered between 1982 and 1984 by Suresh Srivastava of the Geological Survey of India.
The 2003 description relied on a partial skeleton including the braincase, spine, hip, legs, and tail, marking the first time such post-cranial remains were preserved for an Indian theropod.
The fossil history for Rajasaurus began in 1981 when geologists found dinosaur eggs in cement mine balls.
Rajasaurus was likely an ambush predator, similar to other abelisaurids, using a bite-and-hold strategy to hunt large prey.
It likely possessed a bite force of approximately 3500 Newtons, a strength comparable to Allosaurus.
Comparatively short leg bones suggest Rajasaurus was slower than similar-sized theropods.
Researchers suggest the horn was used for display or head-butting other individuals of the same species, involving low-momentum pushes or focused strikes on the neck and flank.
In 2003, Wilson classified Rajasaurus in the subfamily Carnotaurinae, a grouping that demonstrates the widespread global distribution of this group of dinosaurs.
In 2014, paleontologist Thierry Tortosa established the subfamily Majungasaurinae to group Rajasaurus with other abelisaurids based on elongated antorbital fenestrae and a triangular sagittal crest.
Rajasaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Maastrichtian age, approximately 66 million years ago, in what is now the Indian Subcontinent.

Fossils were found in the Lameta Formation in Gujarat, Western India, a site first discovered in 1981 by geologists G. N. Dwivedi and Dhananjay Mahendrakumar Mohabey of the Geological Survey of India.
Rajasaurus closely resembled the abelisaurid Majungasaurus from Madagascar, despite a time separation of 20 million years.
It is debated whether Rajasaurus, Lametasaurus, and Indosaurus are synonymous species, though this remains unconfirmed due to fragmentary remains and the loss of the Lametasaurus specimen.
Hypotheses suggest abelisaurid migration between Europe and India occurred via Africa or through island-hopping along the Dras-Kohistan volcanic arc, though these explanations remain questionable.
